title: The Role of the µ-Opioid Receptor 1 A118G Nucleotide Polymorphism in the Context of Traumatic Childhood Events and Aggression
summary:
Aggression is a complex behavior that is closely linked to human evolution and can have many different causes. In some situations, like protecting yourself or others from danger, aggression can even be justified. But it becomes a problem when it's used inappropriately—such as using violence to gain material things, fulfill personal needs, or even for enjoyment.
How often someone behaves aggressively can be influenced by many things: personal experiences during childhood, their social environment, personality traits, and even their genetic makeup.
This study focuses on patients in a forensic psychiatric facility. These individuals have been placed there because of crimes committed in connection with their substance addiction. The research aims to find out how different versions of a specific brain receptor—called the mu-opioid receptor—are linked to aggressive behavior. It also looks at how difficult experiences in childhood might affect this connection.
Participants are asked to fill out questionnaires about their childhood and their behavior. The reason for looking at this particular brain receptor is that some versions of it may change how certain chemicals are released in the brain—chemicals that can influence how we behave.
To figure out which version of the receptor someone has, a simple cheek swab is taken using a cotton swab. The cells collected from this swab are then analyzed in a lab. The results are compared with the answers from the questionnaires.
Over a period of up to six and a half years, researchers will also observe whether certain versions of the mu-opioid receptor are linked to more frequent failures in therapy. This could help us understand whether genetics play a role in how well people respond to treatment.
conditions: Mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance use

interventions.name:
80 to 160 forensic psychiatric patients undergoing treatment in a detoxification facility according to Section 64 of the German Penal Code (StGB).
